notes:
Based on my research across the approved sources, here are my verse-by-verse notes on Acts 21:

---

## Acts 21 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Departure from Miletus

The Greek verb translated "torn ourselves away" (ἀποσπάω) is emphatic—it means to be plucked or dragged away, conveying the deep emotional pain of parting from the Ephesian elders (see Acts 20:37–38). Chrysostom said it means "had torn away." They sailed a straight course to Cos (an island famous for its medical school and the birthplace of Hippocrates), then the next day to Rhodes (formerly home of the Colossus, one of the seven wonders, now fallen), then to Patara on the Lycian mainland. They were traveling in a small "coasting vessel" unsuited for open-sea travel, which explains the need to change ships at Patara.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/21.htm (v.1); https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.1); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/21.htm (v.1); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.1–2)

### v. 2 — Finding a ship to Phoenicia

The verb "finding" (εὑρίσκω) implies a search. At Patara they found a larger merchant vessel capable of the ~400-mile open-sea crossing to Phoenicia. Sir William Ramsay notes that summer winds in the Aegean blow from the north in the morning and die at sunset, followed by a gentle south breeze—which explains the overnight stops and the need for a larger ship for the open-sea leg.

- **URLs:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.2); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.1–2)

### v. 3 — Sailing past Cyprus, landing at Tyre

As they sailed, Cyprus came into sight—Luke uses the nautical term ἀναφαίνω ("to raise the land"), meaning they sighted it but passed it on the port (left) side without stopping. This would have stirred Paul's memories of his first missionary journey (Acts 13:4–13). They landed at Tyre, the ancient Phoenician port, where the ship had to unload cargo—a process that took seven days, indicating a large shipment.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/21.htm (v.3); https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.3)

### v. 4 — The disciples at Tyre warn Paul "through the Spirit"

The word "finding" implies they searched for believers in the busy port city. The church at Tyre was likely planted when persecuted believers scattered after Stephen's martyrdom (Acts 11:19). They stayed seven days, which Ellicott says was for attending the Lord's Supper on the Lord's Day (as at Troas, Acts 20:6, and later at Puteoli, Acts 28:14).

**The key interpretive issue:** The disciples "through the Spirit" told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. This creates an apparent tension—was Paul disobeying the Holy Spirit?

- **Traditional/Evangelical view (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill, Constable):** The Spirit revealed the *danger* awaiting Paul, but the disciples added their own human application ("therefore, don't go"). The Spirit's purpose was to *prepare* Paul, not to *prohibit* him. Paul was "bound in the spirit" to go (Acts 20:22). Ellicott explains: prophets received the Spirit "by measure" and could foresee danger but lacked the higher inspiration that guided Paul's decision (cf. 2 Timothy 1:7, "spirit…of a sound mind"). Gill says the disciples "by the spirit of prophecy, knew that if the apostle went to Jerusalem, many evil things would befall him; wherefore of their own spirit, and out of love to him, they advise him not to go."

- **Minority view (Gaebelein, dispensational):** Gaebelein takes the record at face value—"the Holy Spirit through these disciples warned the Apostle…that he should not go to Jerusalem…so great was his desire to be in Jerusalem that he ignored the voice of the Spirit." This view holds Paul was genuinely disobedient and his imprisonment was chastisement.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.3–4); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.4); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts-21.htm (v.4); https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.4); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/acts-21.html (Gaebelein); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-21.html (Constable)

### v. 5 — Departure from Tyre, kneeling on the beach

The whole church—men, women, and children—escorted Paul's company out of the city to the shore. This is the first time children are mentioned in connection with apostolic churches (Precept Austin). Kneeling on the shore for prayer followed Jewish custom of using seashores as places of prayer (a *proseuchè*). Ellicott notes the plural suggests Paul was not the only one praying; others (including Luke and Tyrian leaders) joined in reciprocal intercession.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.5); https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.5); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.5–6)

### v. 6 — Farewell and boarding

"They returned home again" uses the Greek idiom εἰς τὰ ἴδια ("to their own"), the same phrase used in John 1:11 ("He came to His own"), John 16:32, and John 19:27. Ellicott notes the article "the ship" likely indicates they re-boarded the same vessel that brought them, now continuing toward Caesarea.

- **URLs:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.6); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.6)

### v. 7 — Ptolemais

Ptolemais (Old Testament Accho, modern Acre/St. Jean d'Acre) was about 32 miles south of Tyre. The ship apparently put in for the night, giving Paul's company time to greet the brethren and stay one day. A church already existed there, probably founded by Philip the evangelist's labors along the coast.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.7); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts-21.htm (v.7)

### v. 8 — Caesarea and Philip the evangelist

Caesarea was about 40 miles farther south. This was Paul's third visit there (cf. Acts 9:30; 18:22). Philip—not the apostle but one of the Seven (Acts 6:5)—had settled there some 20 years earlier after evangelizing the coastal plain (Acts 8:40). His title "the evangelist" (Ephesians 4:11) shows his ministry had grown beyond the original diaconal role of "serving tables" into missionary preaching.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.8); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.8–9); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-21.html (Constable)

### v. 9 — Philip's four prophesying daughters

**Traditional reading:** Philip had four virgin (unmarried) daughters who exercised the gift of prophecy. Ellicott notes that "virgins" probably indicated not just being unmarried but a devoted purpose—an early form of consecrated single life, complementing the order of widows (1 Timothy 5:10). The fact that they "prophesied" included more than predicting the future; it encompassed Spirit-inspired utterance—in other words, they preached.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis (Sam Storms; Pneuma Review):** This verse is a key proof-text for women prophesying. Storms argues: (1) There are no gender restrictions on the gift of prophecy (cf. Acts 2:17–18); (2) Paul's restrictions on women teaching (1 Corinthians 14:34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12) govern the *formal teaching office*, not prophecy, because teaching authority (exposition of Scripture) is distinct from prophetic authority (spontaneous revelation); (3) Philip's daughters being "virgins" does not imply sexual purity is required for prophecy—married women also prophesied (1 Corinthians 11:5). The Pneuma Review discusses how Pentecostal-charismatic traditions see this passage as supporting women in ministry, though noting a "dialectic or paradox" between Spirit-empowerment theology and actual practice in some denominations.

**Reformed/Evangelical (The Gospel Coalition Canada):** Affirms that women can be prophets—"beyond all reasonable dispute." Prophets operate outside the normal hierarchy of the covenant community.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.9); https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/prophecy-in-real-life--acts-21:1-16--27-36-; http://pneumareview.com/philips-daughters/; https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/daughters-philip-agabus-gift-prophecy/

### v. 10 — Agabus arrives

Agabus, last seen in Acts 11:28 predicting a famine, came down from Judea to Caesarea. The stay was "many days" (comparative in Greek: longer than intended), likely because the voyage had been quicker than expected and there was time before Pentecost.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.10); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.10–14)

### v. 11 — Agabus's prophetic sign-act

Agabus took Paul's belt (girdle), bound his own hands and feet, and declared "Thus says the Holy Spirit." This dramatic sign-act followed Old Testament prophetic tradition (Isaiah 20:3–4 walking naked; Jeremiah 13:1–11 burying a girdle; Jeremiah 27:2 making bonds and yokes; Ezekiel 4–5 acting out Jerusalem's siege).

**Key note on the prophecy's fulfillment (Precept Austin):** Agabus said "the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man…and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles." Literally, the Jews did *not* bind Paul—the Romans did (v.33). However, the Jews' actions *resulted* in Paul being arrested by Gentiles, so the prophecy was fulfilled in substance: the Jews were the instigating cause.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.11); https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-21-commentary (v.11); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.10–14)

### v. 12 — Everyone pleads with Paul

For the first time, even Paul's traveling companions—including Luke himself—joined the local believers in begging Paul not to go. They wept. Ellicott notes they may have suggested Paul stay behind in Caesarea while others delivered the Gentile collection to James.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.12); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.10–14)

### v. 13 — Paul's response: ready to die

Paul's emotional response reveals his tender nature—"What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" This was not Stoic hardness; their tears genuinely crushed him. Yet he was ready "not only to be bound, but also to die." Enduring Word quotes Chambers: "No healthy saint ever chooses suffering; he chooses God's will, as Jesus did, whether it means suffering or not."

**Denominational note:** This verse is used broadly across traditions to illustrate costly discipleship. The emphasis on Paul's resolve resonates across Baptist, Reformed, Pentecostal, and Methodist traditions without significant disagreement.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.10–14); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.13)

### v. 14 — "The will of the Lord be done"

Ellicott cautiously suggests these words may not indicate full acceptance that Paul's course *was* God's will, but rather "the natural expressions of resignation to what was seen to be inevitable, possibly used as a quotation from the prayer which the Lord had taught the disciples, and which He had used Himself (Luke 22:42)." Enduring Word and Constable take the stronger view: the companions came to recognize that Paul's determination *was* the Lord's will. Constable draws the parallel with Jesus in Gethsemane: Paul faces the same decision—escape or surrender to God's will.

**Dr. Constable (Dallas Seminary/Evangelical):** Why did Paul avoid death in Corinth (Acts 20:3) but not here? Because dying on a ship would have thwarted his purpose of delivering the collection. Arrest in Jerusalem would not frustrate that purpose—it would advance the gospel in new ways.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.10–14); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.14); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-21.html (Constable)

### v. 15 — Packing up for Jerusalem

"Packed up" (KJV "took up our carriages") refers to baggage or luggage, not vehicles—an archaic English usage (cf. 1 Samuel 17:22). The road from Caesarea to Jerusalem was about 65 miles, a two-to-three-day journey.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.15)

### v. 16 — Mnason of Cyprus

Some Caesarean disciples accompanied Paul and brought him to stay with Mnason, a Cypriot and "early disciple" (ἀρχαίῳ μαθητῇ). This means he had been a disciple "from the beginning"—likely one of the earliest converts, perhaps among those "men of Cyprus" who first preached to Gentiles at Antioch (Acts 11:20). Ellicott suggests Mnason may have been one of Luke's informants for his Gospel (Luke 1:2). He had a house in Jerusalem, providing Paul a safer lodging.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.16); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.15–16)

### v. 17 — Warm welcome in Jerusalem

The "brethren received us gladly"—an informal welcome at Mnason's house before the formal meeting with church leadership.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.17); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.17–20a)

### v. 18 — Meeting with James and the elders

"The next day" probably places this near the Day of Pentecost (see Acts 20:16). James (the Lord's brother) was the recognized leader of the Jerusalem church—Ellicott calls him "the Bishop of Jerusalem" using the later title. "All the elders were present," indicating the full leadership council. Notably, none of the Twelve apostles are mentioned.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.18); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.17–20a)

### v. 19 — Paul's detailed report

Paul "recounted one by one" (καθ' ἓν ἕκαστον) what God had done among the Gentiles. This was a detailed, point-by-point report, not a mere summary. It would have included the Gentile collection he was delivering.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.17–20a); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.19)

### vv. 20–21 — The Jerusalem problem: thousands of zealous Jewish believers

The elders "glorified God" for the Gentile mission, then immediately raised a serious concern. There were "myriads" (tens of thousands) of Jewish believers in Jerusalem, all "zealous for the law" (the Greek term ζηλωταὶ, "zealots," was almost technical for the most rigid Pharisaic party—Ellicott). These believers had heard that Paul taught diaspora Jews "to forsake Moses"—specifically, not to circumcise their children or observe Jewish customs.

Ellicott probes the truth of the accusation: it was false as a *personal* charge—Paul had circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), taken a Nazirite vow himself (Acts 18:18), and taught everyone should remain as they were called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). But the *tendency* of his teaching that "circumcision is nothing" (1 Corinthians 7:19; Galatians 5:6) did undermine the practice. "If a Jew had asked, Why then should I circumcise my child? it would not have been easy to return a satisfying answer."

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (vv.20–21); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.20b–22)

### v. 22 — "What then should we do?"

This has the sense, "This is controversial, people will hear you've arrived—we need a plan." The "assembly must certainly meet" (KJV) likely refers to an inevitable public confrontation unless action was taken.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.20b–22)

### vv. 23–24 — The plan: sponsor four men under a Nazirite vow

The Jerusalem elders proposed that Paul join four men who had taken a vow (almost certainly a Nazirite vow—Numbers 6:1–21), purify himself with them, and pay their expenses (including the required animal sacrifices). This would publicly demonstrate that Paul himself "lives in obedience to the law."

**The debate over Paul's participation:** This is one of the most discussed passages in Acts.

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic leaning):** Paul's sponsorship was not compromise but flexibility. Citing Adam Clarke: "He had shown them that their ceremonies were useless but not destructive; that they were only dangerous when they depended on them for salvation." Paul was practicing 1 Corinthians 9:20—"to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews." The animal sacrifices involved were not for atonement (only Christ's sacrifice atones) but offerings for thanksgiving or dedication.

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** The question is whether Paul was right to comply. Ellicott argues that Paul's principle of "becoming all things to all men" justified the action, but acknowledges that the plan ultimately failed to prevent the riot.

- **Reformed/Evangelical (Ligonier, The Gospel Coalition):** (I was unable to find a dedicated Reformed treatment of this specific passage within the search limits.)

**Lutheran view:** No dedicated Lutheran page on this passage was found within search limits.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.23–25); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (implied in v.21 discussion)

### v. 25 — The Gentile believers exempted

The elders reaffirmed the Apostolic Decree (Acts 15:20, 29): Gentile believers need only abstain from food sacrificed to idols, blood, meat of strangled animals, and sexual immorality. This was a crucial clarification—Paul's participation in the vow did NOT mean Gentiles must keep the Law. Enduring Word emphasizes Paul "would rightly refuse to compromise on this important point."

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.23–25)

### v. 26 — Paul enters the temple

Paul took the men, purified himself, and entered the temple to give notice of the purification period's completion date, when offerings would be made for each. The purification lasted seven days.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.26)

### vv. 27–29 — The riot: Jews from Asia seize Paul

Near the end of the seven days, "Jews from the province of Asia" (probably from Ephesus) recognized Paul in the temple and stirred up the crowd. Their charges echoed those against Stephen (Acts 6:13): teaching against "the people" (Israel), "the law," and "this place" (the temple). The added charge—bringing Greeks into the temple—was based on assumption: they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian (Acts 20:4) with Paul in the city and *supposed* Paul brought him into the temple.

Enduring Word notes signs posted in the temple Court of the Gentiles read (in Greek and Latin): "No foreigner may enter within the barricade which surrounds the temple and enclosure. Anyone who is caught trespassing will bear personal responsibility for his ensuing death." The Romans authorized the Jews to execute violators, even Roman citizens.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.27–30); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghc/acts-21.html (Hampton)

### v. 30 — Dragged out, gates shut

The mob dragged Paul from the inner courts to the Court of the Gentiles and "at once the gates were shut"—likely the gates between the Court of the Gentiles and the inner courts, to prevent bloodshed from defiling the holy place.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.27–30); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghc/acts-21.html

### vv. 31–32 — Roman intervention

The Roman commander (χιλίαρχος, tribune) of the cohort stationed at the Tower of Antonia—over 500 soldiers just two flights of stairs from the Court of the Gentiles—received word of the uproar and rushed down with soldiers and centurions. The mob stopped beating Paul when they saw the troops.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.31–36)

### v. 33 — Bound with two chains

Paul was bound with two chains—likely handcuffed to a soldier on each side (cf. Acts 12:6; 28:16). This moment fulfilled Agabus's prophecy (v.11). The commander then asked who Paul was and what he had done.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.31–36); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.33)

### v. 34 — Confusion and the barracks

The crowd shouted contradictory answers (paralleling the confused clamor at Ephesus, Acts 19:32, described in identical terms). Unable to determine the truth, the commander ordered Paul taken into the barracks (the Tower of Antonia).

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.34)

### vv. 35–36 — Carried by soldiers; "Away with him!"

The violence of the mob was so great that soldiers had to physically carry Paul up the stairs. The crowd shouted "Away with him!"—the same cry with which Jesus' death had been demanded about 27 years earlier near the same spot (Luke 23:18; John 19:15). Boice notes: "They did not mean, 'Take him away from the temple area.' They meant, 'Remove him from the earth.' They wanted him dead." Bruce draws the parallel to Jesus' passion.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.31–36); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.35)

### vv. 37–38 — Paul addresses the commander in Greek

The commander was startled that Paul spoke Greek—he had assumed Paul was "the Egyptian" who led 4,000 "Assassins" (Sicarii, dagger-men) into the wilderness. Josephus records this Egyptian false prophet had gathered followers on the Mount of Olives promising to overthrow Jerusalem's walls; Roman troops scattered them but the leader escaped. Paul's polite, educated Greek immediately changed the commander's assessment.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.37–39); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.37–38)

### v. 39 — Paul identifies himself

"I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city." Tarsus was a renowned center of learning (Strabo said it rivaled Athens and Alexandria). This identification elevated Paul from suspected terrorist to respectable citizen.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.37–39)

### v. 40 — Paul addresses the crowd in Hebrew

Receiving permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned for silence. "A great hush came over the crowd"—the same crowd that moments before had been screaming for his death. He spoke "in Hebrew" (Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ), meaning Aramaic, the common language of Judean Jews. Ellicott notes the irony: the commander expected Hebrew and heard Greek; the crowd expected Greek and heard Hebrew—demonstrating Jerusalem's bilingual character.

Enduring Word emphasizes that even beaten and in chains, Paul's first thought was to preach the gospel.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-21/ (v.40); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-21.htm (v.40)

---

## Denominational Distinctives Summary

| Issue | Traditions | Key Difference |
|-------|------------|----------------|
| **v.4 – The Spirit's warning** | Evangelical majority (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill, Constable) vs. Dispensational (Gaebelein) | Was the Spirit *preparing* Paul or *prohibiting* him? Majority: preparing; Gaebelein: prohibiting, Paul was disobedient |
| **v.9 – Women prophesying** | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Sam Storms, Pneuma Review) vs. some complementarian Reformed | All agree women can prophesy. Pentecostals use this to support broader women's ministry; complementarians distinguish prophecy from the teaching office |
| **vv.23–26 – Paul's vow participation** | Broad evangelical agreement | Most see it as legitimate contextualization (1 Cor 9:20), not compromise. Some older commentators (and some modern critics) consider it a failure of nerve |

**Views not found within search limits:** Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Baptist-specific (spurgeon.org, desiringgod.org, gty.org), and modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) were not returned in search results for Acts 21–specific content. The "word of faith" or "prosperity" teaching on this passage was also not found in the searches.
